02General notesHAS-001 · Sheet 02 / 11

General notes

Every note is tagged with the browsers it applies to.

  1. All browsers When something changes, the browser walks up from the changed element and re-checks the :has() anchors above it whose rules the change touches.
  2. All browsers A rule that styles its own anchor restyles one element per re-check.
  3. All browsers A rule that styles things inside its anchor restyles its targets under that anchor. Even when the match didn’t change.
  4. Chrome Re-checks every anchor above the change, whether or not its rule mentions it. For pseudo-class changes, any anchor whose :has() has a pseudo-class.
  5. Chrome Merges the targets of every rule that styles inside its anchor into one shared list, and each re-checked anchor restyles all of it. One * makes the list “everything”.
  6. All browsers So the expensive shape is a big anchor (body, main, a page wrapper) with a rule that styles things inside it. Scoping helps everywhere; Chrome gains the most.

All browsers means Chrome, Firefox and Safari. Chrome also covers the other Chromium browsers: Edge, Arc, Opera and friends. Simplified for clarity: with :has(+ …) and :has(~ …), the walk also visits earlier siblings.

03AnatomyHAS-001 · Sheet 03 / 11

Anatomy of a :has() rule

Three words do all the work on this site.

Anchor
The element the :has() is attached to.
Condition
What’s inside the parentheses. It’s what the browser listens for.
Target
What the rule actually styles: the anchor itself, or something inside it.

Chromium’s names for these are “subject” and “non-subject” :has().

04The processHAS-001 · Sheet 04 / 11

What happens on every change

Every browser runs the same loop. The red notes are where Chrome does more. Pick a change to light up its path.

Follow one change

The rule: .tab:has(.category-item.active). It styles .tab itself.

  1. Start.active is added to a .category-item.
  2. D1.active is in the rule’s condition. Yes, so start walking.
  3. D2The item has a parent: .tab. Step up to it.
  4. D3.tab is the rule’s anchor. Yes.
  5. D4The rule styles the anchor, so mark .tab.
  6. LoopKeep walking up through main, body and html. None of them anchor the rule.
  7. Endhtml has no parent, so restyle everything marked: just .tab.

The rule: main:has(.category-item.active) button. It styles the buttons inside main.

  1. Start.active is added to a .category-item.
  2. D1.active is in the rule’s condition. Yes, so start walking.
  3. D2Step up to the item’s parent, .tab.
  4. D3.tab doesn’t anchor the rule. No, so keep walking.
  5. D2Step up to main.
  6. D3main is the rule’s anchor. Yes.
  7. D4The rule styles things inside, so mark every button in main.
  8. EndPast body and html, restyle everything marked: every button in the page, near the change or not.

The rule: .tab:has(.category-item.active).

  1. Start.open is added to a .category-item.
  2. D1.open isn’t in any :has() condition. No.
  3. EndNothing to do: no walk, nothing marked, nothing restyled.

Two rules: .tab:has(.category-item.active) and main:has(.promo). Both style their anchor.

  1. Start.active is added to a .category-item.
  2. D1.active is in .tab’s condition. Yes, so start walking.
  3. D2–D4Step up to .tab. It anchors that rule and styles itself, so mark .tab.
  4. D3Step up to main. Its rule is about .promo, not .active. Firefox and Safari say no. Chrome says yes: any anchor counts.
  5. D4In Chrome, main’s rule styles main itself, so mark main too.
  6. EndChrome restyles .tab and main. Firefox and Safari restyle just .tab.

The whole loop, every path at once. Point at any box to light up where it leads and what leads to it.

D3 is where browsers differ most: Firefox and Safari only re-check anchors whose own rule mentions the change.

05Lesson 1 · Rule shapeHAS-001 · Sheet 05 / 11

What the rule styles sets the blast radius

All browsers One change, four rules, one rule at a time. Every browser gives the same answer here: try the switch.

  • Styles itself: one element, however big the anchor. 1A · 1C
  • Styles inside: its targets inside the anchor, near the change or not. 1B · 1D
  • A big anchor that styles inside is the shape that sweeps the page. 1D
06Lesson 2 · Chrome’s extra workHAS-001 · Sheet 06 / 11

Chrome re-checks more, and shares the list

Chrome Two rules on the page this time. Flip the switch: Firefox and Safari skip all three of these.

  • Re-checks unrelated anchors: ones whose rule doesn’t mention the change. 2A
  • Shares one list: a re-checked anchor restyles every such rule’s targets. 2B
  • One * anywhere makes that list “everything”. 2C
07Lesson 3 · Pseudo-classesHAS-001 · Sheet 07 / 11

Chrome’s pseudo-class filter

Chrome For :hover, :checked, :focus and friends.

  • No pseudo-class in an anchor’s :has(): Chrome skips it. 3A
  • Any pseudo-class in it: Chrome re-checks it, even a different one. 3B
  • Firefox and Safari only re-check rules that mention the pseudo-class that changed.
08Lesson 4 · DirectionHAS-001 · Sheet 08 / 11

It only walks up

All browsers The same in every browser.

  • The walk only goes up from the element that changed.
  • Anchors that aren’t above it are never visited, whatever their rules say. 4A
09MeasuredHAS-001 · Sheet 09 / 11

Measured in Chrome, Firefox and Safari

The spec only defines what :has() matches. How a browser works out what to restyle after a change is up to the browser, so we ran the same tests in all three. main holds 20,000 .nav-links, so any sweep of main is easy to spot.

Every browser

  • A change that touches a rule’s condition (a class, attribute or pseudo-class in it, or a matching element added or removed) re-checks that rule’s anchors and restyles its targets. Even when the match doesn’t change.
  • So a big anchor that styles things inside it is expensive everywhere. Firefox and Safari spent longer on those restyles than Chrome did.

Chrome only

  • Re-checking anchors whose rule doesn’t mention the change.
  • The shared list: one rule’s targets restyled by another anchor’s re-check.
  • Any pseudo-class in an anchor’s :has() being enough.
  • A * in one rule widening every other anchor’s re-check.

Chrome 156 is the stable release, run directly; Chrome Canary 159 matched it within half a millisecond on every row. Firefox 157 and WebKit 27.2 are Playwright’s builds of those engines; WebKit 27.2 is a little ahead of the shipping Safari 26.6. Measured November 2026. Each link has an inline style, so no browser can share one computed style between them. Each figure is the median of five batches of 40 changes, with a full style and layout update after every change. Pseudo-class rows use :checked, because a script can’t fake a real hover. Firefox and Safari do skip some insertions that can’t change the result, like a match added right next to an existing one. Compare within a column: absolute numbers vary by browser and machine.

10Rules of thumbHAS-001 · Sheet 10 / 11

Rules of thumb

Every one of these helps in every browser. Chrome gains the most, because it re-checks more anchors and shares one to-do list.

  1. Prefer rules that style the anchor itself

    .card:has(.badge) { … } restyles one element per re-check, wherever it lives.

    Helps everywhere

  2. Anchor on the smallest element you can

    The smallest element that contains both the condition and the target: fewer changes reach it, and less sits under it.

    Helps everywhereChrome gains most

  3. Keep big anchors from styling inside

    No body, html, main or page wrapper anchoring a rule that styles things inside it. Put the state on the root as an attribute, written by the code that changes it: html[data-menu-open] .header { … }.

    Helps everywhereChrome gains most

  4. No trailing *

    A * target restyles the anchor’s whole subtree on every re-check. In Chrome it widens every other anchor’s re-check too.

    Helps everywhereChrome gains most

  5. Count your :has() rules together

    Each rule adds re-checks. In Chrome they also share one to-do list, so count them as a set, especially in global stylesheets.

    Helps everywhereChrome gains most

  6. Check it

    Chrome: DevTools → Performance → record the interaction → Recalculate Style → Elements affected. Safari’s Timelines and the Firefox Profiler show style recalculations too.

    Every browser

11SourcesHAS-001 · Sheet 11 / 11

Sources

Chrome’s behaviour comes from Chromium’s source at dc5f947, November 2026. Firefox’s and Safari’s comes from measuring them.

  • Selectors Level 4 · :has()The spec: what :has() matches. How browsers invalidate it is up to them.
  • style_engine.cc L1585Chrome: pseudo-class walks skip anchors with no pseudo-class in their :has().
  • style_engine.cc L1591Chrome: “mutation of class value ‘d’ can invalidate ancestor with class value ‘a’”, no per-rule filtering.
  • style_engine.cc L1595Chrome: styles itself, so restyle the anchor.
  • style_engine.cc L1605Chrome: styles inside, so apply one invalidation set for the whole :has pseudo-class.
  • rule_invalidation_data.h L234Chrome: those sets are kept per pseudo-class type, not per rule.
  • style_engine.cc L2059Chrome: where pseudo-class changes start their walk.
  • element.cc L13571Chrome: :hover goes through the same pseudo-class path.
  • Sheet 09 · MeasuredChrome 156 and Canary 159 alongside Firefox 157 and WebKit 27.2, November 2026.
